tracks.title: Climate change and extreme weather
tracks.note: BBC 기상캐스터 Sarah Keith-Lucas와 함께 기후변화가 태풍·허리케인 같은 극한 날씨를 어떻게 바꾸는지 이야기해요. 태풍이 느려지면 비와 바람이 더 오래 머물고, 해수면 상승으로 storm surge(폭풍 해일)가 더 위험해진대요. 1회차는 대략적인 내용만, 2회차는 스크립트를 보면서 들어요.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Hello, this is 6 Minute English from BBC Learning English.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I'm Phil.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: It seems that we're hearing about more and more terrible weather, but how exactly is climate change affecting extreme weather?

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I'm lucky today to be joined by BBC Weather forecaster, meteorologist and presenter, Sarah Keith-Lucas.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Hi Sarah.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Hi Phil.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: It's great to be here.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Sarah's here to help us understand what's happening with extreme weather.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: She'll also help explain some of the words and expressions used in a new series of BBC Learning English videos all about weather and climate and the language we use to talk about them.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: You can find the link to them on our webpage, or in the show notes for this podcast.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Sarah, let’s start with a really important question: what’s the difference between climate and weather?

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: That’s a great question, Phil.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: The weather is what you see and feel every day.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Climate is more long-term.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Today I’ll explain how a change in the climate over the long term can be seen in the weather.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: As always, we will also be learning some key vocabulary to talk about the topic.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: And, Sarah, it’s traditional for us to set a quiz question.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Have you got one for us?

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Yes, I have!

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: By how much has Earth's temperature increased since 1970.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Is it? a) Around 0.5C b) Around 1C c) Around 2C

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I don't know, about 2 degrees?

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: I'll give the answer at the end of the programme, so listen to the end to find out.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Now, we're going to talk about tropical storms.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: What do we mean by 'tropical storms', Sarah?

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Well, those are hurricanes, cyclones and typhoons.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: They're large rotating storm systems formed over warm tropical waters.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: These are actually the same, we just use different names depending on where in the world they form.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Hurricanes are found in the Atlantic, Cyclones in the Indian Ocean and Typhoons in the West Pacific.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: As the world warms, climate scientists think that these storms will get more destructive.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: In one of our new Learning English for weather videos, meteorologist Darren Bett tells us about another worrying change.

transcript.speaker: Darren Bett
transcript.text: Scientists also think storms are slowing down.

transcript.speaker: Darren Bett
transcript.text: They're not moving across as quickly, and that means if a storm is in the same area for longer, the winds will be stronger for longer, and the rain will last for longer producing more flooding and more likelihood of flooding and landslides and also mudslides.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Darren said that if a storm moves more slowly, there will be more likelihood of flooding.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Likelihood is the noun that we use to say how probable, or how likely something is to happen.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Darren also told us about landslides and mudslides.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Yes, landslides are where a large amount of earth or rock moves down a slope quickly.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Mudslides tend to be faster and more liquid.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Both of these things can happen after particularly heavy rain and can cause damage to buildings.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: People can also be killed or injured by them.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: What else causes loss of life in a hurricane, typhoon or cyclone?

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Well, something else that is very dangerous is a storm surge.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Let's hear again from my colleague Darren Bett.

transcript.speaker: Darren Bett
transcript.text: Storm surge, that's that body of water that gets swept inland and produces widespread flooding.

transcript.speaker: Darren Bett
transcript.text: Climate change is warming our seas, and the sea levels are rising.

transcript.speaker: Darren Bett
transcript.text: That potentially could mean that a storm surge which is one element of a storm that produces more casualties than any other, those storm surges could become even more dangerous.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: So, we had the word casualty, and this is used to talk about people killed or injured by an accident, a military attack, or in this case an extreme weather event.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Darren talked about storm surges.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: A storm surge is where the sea level rises quickly pushed by the strong winds caused by a storm.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: This water comes onto land with an enormous amount lot of force, and storm surges can be up to 10 metres high.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Buildings get destroyed, people can drown.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: We heard about the storm sweeping inland.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Something sweeping in is moving quickly and powerfully.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: And you can hear more from Darren in the videos on our website.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Sarah, how about the answer to the quiz question you asked earlier?

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: OK, Phil.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: So, I asked by how much has the world's average temperature increased since 1970.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: And I thought that it was around two celsius.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: It's actually around one degree celsius.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: 1C is just an average across all of earth's land and ocean surface.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Some places are warming much quicker than this such as the Arctic that's warming 3 times faster than the average rate.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Just a small increase in average temperature can lead to a much bigger increase in extreme events such as heatwaves, wildfires and floods.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Oh wow, so that is an important difference.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: OK, let's recap the vocabulary we've learned, starting with likelihood, which is noun that we use to talk how probable or how likely something is to happen.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Landslides and mudslides which can occur after heavy rainfall make earth or mud move downhill very fast.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: A storm surge is a sudden rise in the sea level, that can move inland causing destruction.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: If something sweeps in, it moves in very fast and very powerfully.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: And finally, a casualty is someone who is injured or killed by an accident, attack, or something like an extreme weather event.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Once again, our six minutes are up.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Goodbye!

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Thank for joining us today, Sarah!

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Bye!

listening.task: 6 Minute English를 한 번은 대략적인 내용만 듣고, 두 번째는 스크립트를 보면서 들어요. 그다음 퀴즈에 답해 보세요. 'likelihood', 'storm surge', 'casualty'가 나오는 부분을 잘 들어 보세요.

quiz.q: By how much has Earth's temperature increased since 1970? a) Around 0.5C, b) Around 1C, c) Around 2C
quiz.answer: b) Around 1C. Phil은 2도라고 했지만 틀렸어요. 1도는 전 지구 평균이고, 북극은 평균보다 3배 빨리 따뜻해지고 있대요. 작은 평균 상승도 폭염·산불·홍수 같은 극한 현상을 크게 늘릴 수 있어요.

sentences.text: The weather is what you see and feel every day.
As the world warms, climate scientists think that these storms will get more destructive.
sentences.ko: 세계가 따뜻해지면서, 기후 과학자들은 이 폭풍들이 더 파괴적이 될 거라고 생각해요.

sentences.text: Scientists also think storms are slowing down.
Oh wow, so that is an important difference.

reading.title: Anthropic's giant IPO puts the heat on OpenAI
reading.source: The Economist (public reprint via Hindustan Times)
reading.summaryKo: ChatGPT로 AI 붐을 연 건 OpenAI지만, 이번 주 사상 최대 규모 IPO(약 900억 달러 조달, 목표 시가총액 1.5조 달러)를 하는 건 OpenAI에서 나온 사람들이 세운 Anthropic이에요. 2단계 경쟁인 '코딩 에이전트'에서 Claude Code가 폭발적으로 성장해 올해 매출 530억 달러 예상(OpenAI는 350억). 다음 경쟁은 모든 사무직 업무로 에이전트를 넓히는 것. OpenAI는 소비자·광고·기기·로봇까지 넓게 벌이고, Anthropic은 기업과 코딩에 집중하며 광고를 하지 않겠다고 했어요. 매일 Claude로 개발하는 입장에서 읽으면 재미있어요.
excerpt: OpenAI may have led the first phase of competition among model-makers, based around chatbots, but Anthropic trounced it in the second phase, where coding agents became the biggest source of business. Claude Code, Anthropic's software-writing bot, was launched in early 2025, but this year has experienced explosive growth.
Nonetheless, the past few years show how quickly leads can be lost in the fast-evolving AI market. Use of OpenAI's own programming tool, Codex, has grown rapidly in recent months.
reading.tip: 'trounce'는 '완패시키다'로, 경쟁 기사에서 beat보다 강한 말이에요. 'Nonetheless'(그럼에도 불구하고)는 앞 내용을 뒤집을 때 쓰는 연결어. 'leads can be lost'처럼 수동태로 일반적인 진실을 말하는 것도 Economist 스타일이에요.

vocab.example: A slower storm means a greater likelihood of flooding.
Storm surges produce more casualties than any other part of a storm.
The water swept inland and caused widespread flooding.
Anthropic trounced OpenAI in the second phase of competition.
Claude Code has experienced explosive growth this year.
OpenAI's revenue was nearly triple that of its arch-rival.
The danger is that it spreads its focus and resources too thinly.

writing.prompt: Write 3–5 sentences in English about how you use AI tools (like Claude) in your work or study.
writing.question: Do you think it's better for a company to focus on one thing, or to try many things? What about you — do you spread yourself too thinly?
writing.hint: 이런 표현을 써 보세요: I use AI tools to ... / It helps me ... / I think focusing on ... is better because ... / Sometimes I spread myself too thinly when ...
